title: Integration tests with Testcontainers
intro: Integration tests verify that multiple real parts of your application work together, including the database, HTTP layer, serialization, transactions, and security configuration. In this lesson, you will see how Spring Boot, Testcontainers, and PostgreSQL can turn those assumptions into repeatable tests.
body:
## What is an integration test?

A unit test isolates a small piece of code. That is useful, but isolation also means some real application problems remain invisible.

An **integration test** checks that multiple parts of an application work together correctly.

For the task manager, an integration test might exercise this path:

~~~text
HTTP request
    ↓
Spring Security
    ↓
Controller
    ↓
JSON mapping
    ↓
Service
    ↓
Repository
    ↓
PostgreSQL
~~~

A unit test for `TaskService` can prove that the service behaves correctly when its repository returns the expected objects. It cannot prove that your JPA query works against the actual PostgreSQL schema.

Integration tests can catch problems such as:

- Incorrect SQL or JPA queries.
- Wrong database column mappings.
- Transaction behaviour that differs from expectations.
- JSON serialization or deserialization problems.
- Incorrect HTTP status codes.
- Security configuration that blocks or exposes an endpoint unexpectedly.
- Database migrations that do not produce the schema your application expects.

The trade-off is that integration tests are slower and require more setup than unit tests.

## @SpringBootTest

Spring Boot provides `@SpringBootTest` for tests that need a large part of the application context.

The **application context** is the collection of Spring-managed objects, configuration, and infrastructure that make up your running application.

A simple test might look like:

~~~java
@SpringBootTest
class TaskApplicationTest {

    @Test
    void applicationStarts() {
        // Spring context loaded successfully.
    }
}
~~~

This is useful when you want to test your application using real Spring configuration.

However, you should not automatically use `@SpringBootTest` for every test. Starting a large application context can be relatively expensive.

Spring provides **test slices** for narrower integration-style tests.

## Test slices

A test slice loads only the part of Spring that you need for a particular type of test.

### @WebMvcTest

`@WebMvcTest` focuses on the Spring MVC web layer. It is useful for testing controllers without starting the entire application.

You can use **MockMvc**, a Spring testing tool that sends simulated HTTP requests through the MVC infrastructure:

~~~java
@WebMvcTest(TaskController.class)
class TaskControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    MockMvc mockMvc;

    @Test
    void returnsTasks() throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(get("/api/tasks"))
            .andExpect(status().isOk());
    }
}
~~~

This tests the HTTP layer without requiring a real network server.

### @DataJpaTest

`@DataJpaTest` focuses on JPA and database-related components.

It is useful for testing repositories and persistence mappings. For example, you can verify that a repository query returns the expected tasks from a real test database.

A slice test is a useful middle ground: more realistic than a pure unit test, but smaller and faster than starting the entire application.

## Why use Testcontainers?

A major problem with database integration tests is the database itself.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "A real database for every test run", "nodes": [{"id": "t", "label": "@SpringBootTest", "kind": "code"}, {"id": "tc", "label": "Testcontainers", "sub": "starts postgres:16 in Docker", "kind": "service", "highlight": true}, {"id": "fw", "label": "Flyway", "sub": "V1…Vn migrations", "kind": "file", "col": 1}, {"id": "api", "label": "MockMvc → API", "kind": "server", "col": 1}, {"id": "db", "label": "Throwaway PostgreSQL", "kind": "db", "highlight": true}], "edges": [{"from": "t", "to": "tc", "label": "starts"}, {"from": "tc", "to": "db", "label": "@ServiceConnection"}, {"from": "fw", "to": "db", "label": "migrates"}, {"from": "t", "to": "api", "label": "HTTP calls"}, {"from": "api", "to": "db", "dashed": true}]}
~~~

You could use an in-memory database such as H2, but H2 and PostgreSQL are different database engines. A query or constraint that works in H2 may behave differently in PostgreSQL.

**Testcontainers** lets your tests start real services inside Docker containers.

For our application, that means the test can start a real PostgreSQL database:

~~~text
JUnit test
    ↓
Testcontainers
    ↓
PostgreSQL Docker container
    ↓
real SQL / schema / transactions
~~~

This makes the test environment much closer to the production database.

You do not have to manually install a separate PostgreSQL database for the test suite. Testcontainers manages the container lifecycle for the test.

Docker must be running for this approach to work.

## @Testcontainers and @Container

Testcontainers integrates with JUnit using annotations such as `@Testcontainers` and `@Container`.

A simplified PostgreSQL example is:

~~~java
@Testcontainers
class TaskRepositoryTest {

    @Container
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16");

    @Test
    void storesTask() {
        // test database is running
    }
}
~~~

`@Testcontainers` enables Testcontainers' JUnit integration.

`@Container` marks the container whose lifecycle should be managed for the test.

The exact PostgreSQL image version should be chosen deliberately for your project rather than blindly copying an example. In a real project, using a version close to your production PostgreSQL version reduces compatibility surprises.

## @ServiceConnection in Spring Boot 3.1+

Spring Boot 3.1 introduced `@ServiceConnection`, which makes connecting Spring Boot to supported Testcontainers services much simpler.

For example:

~~~java
@Testcontainers
@SpringBootTest
class TaskIntegrationTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16");
}
~~~

Spring Boot can use the container's connection information to configure the relevant application connection automatically.

This avoids manually copying dynamically assigned container host and port information into test properties.

The result is a clean relationship:

~~~text
Testcontainers starts PostgreSQL
        ↓
@ServiceConnection supplies connection details
        ↓
Spring Boot configures DataSource
        ↓
Application talks to the real container
~~~

## Flyway migrations in tests

Our production application uses database migrations. **Flyway** is a database migration tool that applies versioned schema changes in a controlled order.

For example:

~~~text
V1__create_users.sql
V2__create_tasks.sql
V3__add_task_indexes.sql
~~~

A strong integration test environment should run the same migrations against the test database rather than silently creating a different schema.

The flow becomes:

~~~text
Start PostgreSQL container
        ↓
Flyway runs migrations
        ↓
Expected schema exists
        ↓
Spring Boot starts
        ↓
Integration test runs
~~~

This can catch migration problems before deployment.

For example, suppose your Java entity expects an `owner_id` column but the migration accidentally creates `user_id`. A unit test may never notice. A real integration test using the migrated database can expose the mismatch.

## Testing REST endpoints

Integration tests become especially useful when you exercise an endpoint and inspect the response.

With MockMvc, you can test the HTTP contract without starting a real browser.

For example:

~~~java
mockMvc.perform(
        post("/api/tasks")
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .content("{\"title\":\"Learn testing\"}"))
    .andExpect(status().isCreated())
    .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Learn testing"));
~~~

This checks more than a service unit test:

- The route exists.
- JSON can be deserialized.
- Validation works.
- The controller calls the application correctly.
- The response has the expected status.
- JSON serialization produces the expected structure.

You can also test invalid requests:

~~~java
mockMvc.perform(
        post("/api/tasks")
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .content("{\"title\":\"\"}"))
    .andExpect(status().isBadRequest());
~~~

A **400 Bad Request** tells the client that the request itself is invalid.

## MockMvc versus TestRestTemplate

MockMvc exercises Spring MVC without requiring an actual HTTP server port.

Another option is `TestRestTemplate`, which can send HTTP requests to a running Spring Boot test application.

Conceptually:

~~~text
MockMvc
Client -> Spring MVC directly

TestRestTemplate
Client -> HTTP -> running Spring Boot server
~~~

`TestRestTemplate` is useful when you want to test the application more like a real HTTP client would. MockMvc is often faster and convenient for web-layer tests.

Choose the level of realism that provides useful confidence for the behaviour you are testing.

## Isolating integration tests

Integration tests interact with stateful systems such as databases. That creates an important question: what happens when one test changes the database?

Suppose test A creates:

~~~text
Task 1
~~~

Then test B expects an empty database. If test A's data remains, test B may pass or fail depending on test order.

This creates a flaky test suite.

Tests should normally start from predictable state.

One strategy is to create fresh database state for each test. Another is to use transactions and roll them back after each test.

## @Transactional and rollback

Spring tests can use `@Transactional` so database changes made during a test are rolled back when the test finishes.

Conceptually:

~~~text
Begin transaction
    ↓
Test changes database
    ↓
Assertions
    ↓
Rollback
    ↓
Database restored
~~~

This can be very convenient.

However, rollback has caveats.

If your application starts another transaction, uses asynchronous processing, communicates with another service, or commits work outside the test transaction, those changes may not be rolled back with the test's transaction.

Also, a test that only passes because of a surrounding transaction may not behave exactly like the production request flow.

For this reason, understand the transaction boundaries rather than treating `@Transactional` as a universal cleanup mechanism.

For important integration tests, explicitly controlling database state can sometimes be clearer.

## Fresh data per test

Another strategy is to seed the database with known data before each test and clean it afterwards.

For example:

~~~text
Before test:
Task A
Task B

Run test

After test:
discard test database/state
~~~

Testcontainers makes this easier when the container or database can be recreated or reset in a controlled way.

The key is isolation: a test should not depend on another test's writes.

## Making integration tests fast enough for CI

Integration tests are slower than unit tests, but that does not mean they have to be painfully slow.

Some practical techniques are:

- Keep unit tests numerous and fast.
- Use test slices when a full application context is unnecessary.
- Reuse containers where safe rather than starting a new Docker container for every test method.
- Keep the test database focused on the required schema and data.
- Avoid unnecessary network calls to external services.
- Run integration tests in parallel only when their isolation is reliable.
- Keep E2E tests separate from the much larger unit and integration suites.

Testcontainers also supports reusable and optimized container strategies, but do not optimize prematurely. First make the tests reliable and isolated, then measure where the time is actually going.

A CI pipeline can therefore have a structure such as:

~~~text
Every push
   ↓
Unit tests
   ↓
Integration tests
   ↓
Build
   ↓
Selected E2E tests
~~~

## Docker must be running

Because Testcontainers uses Docker, Docker needs to be available when the tests run.

~~~callout warn Docker must be running
`Could not find a valid Docker environment` means Docker Desktop is not started. Start it, wait for the whale icon to settle, and re-run the tests.
~~~

If you run the tests locally and Docker is stopped, a Testcontainers PostgreSQL test will fail before it can perform its database assertions.

This is not necessarily an application bug. It may simply mean that the required test infrastructure is unavailable.

The same applies in CI: the CI environment must provide a Docker-compatible environment for Testcontainers to start its containers.

## Common mistakes

### Using H2 when production uses PostgreSQL without thinking about the differences

An in-memory database can be useful, but it does not reproduce every PostgreSQL behaviour. For important database integration tests, a real PostgreSQL container gives stronger confidence.

### Sharing database state between tests

Tests that depend on previous tests are fragile. Seed predictable data and isolate writes so each test can run independently.

### Assuming @Transactional always cleans everything

Transactions only roll back work inside the relevant transaction boundary. Asynchronous work, separate transactions, external services, and other boundaries can escape the rollback.

### Testing only the service layer

A service test cannot prove that JSON mapping, HTTP status codes, routing, validation, migrations, or real SQL all work together. Use integration tests for these boundaries.

### Starting a full application context for every tiny test

If you only need repository behaviour, consider `@DataJpaTest`. If you only need MVC behaviour, consider `@WebMvcTest`. Use `@SpringBootTest` when the broader application context is actually valuable.

### Forgetting Docker

Testcontainers needs Docker. If the test environment cannot start containers, PostgreSQL integration tests cannot run.

## A practical integration-test strategy

For the task manager, use each test level for a different question.

~~~text
Unit test:
“Does this Java method calculate the correct result?”

Web slice test:
“Does this controller return the correct HTTP response?”

JPA integration test:
“Does this repository query work with PostgreSQL?”

Full integration test:
“Does authentication + controller + service + repository + PostgreSQL work together?”

E2E test:
“Can a real user complete this flow through the browser?”
~~~

A good integration test should prove something that would be difficult or impossible to prove with an isolated unit test.

For example, if the task manager has a `POST /api/tasks` endpoint, a valuable integration test can submit JSON, pass through validation and security, save the task to PostgreSQL, and verify the returned JSON.

That one test exercises several boundaries simultaneously.

The goal is not to replace unit tests with integration tests. It is to combine the levels so each one answers the questions it is best suited to answer.
takeaways: Integration tests verify that real application components such as HTTP, JSON, JPA, transactions, security, and PostgreSQL work together.
@SpringBootTest provides a broad application context, while @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest provide focused test slices.
Testcontainers lets your tests use a real PostgreSQL instance in Docker, and @ServiceConnection simplifies Spring Boot configuration.
Tests need isolated data; @Transactional rollback can help, but transaction boundaries and asynchronous work create important caveats.
Integration tests should be reliable and useful enough for CI, with Docker available wherever Testcontainers runs.

quiz.question: What can a PostgreSQL integration test verify that a pure service unit test may not?
options: Only the spelling of Java method names
Real SQL, database mappings, migrations, and database behaviour
Whether TypeScript compiles
Whether the developer's IDE is installed
quiz.explanation: A real database integration test can exercise SQL, JPA mappings, constraints, transactions, and the actual migrated schema, which an isolated service unit test normally cannot.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of @DataJpaTest?
options: To focus testing on JPA and database-related components
To launch Playwright in a browser
To replace PostgreSQL with React
To test only authentication cookies
quiz.explanation: @DataJpaTest is a Spring Boot test slice designed to focus on JPA and persistence-related behaviour.

quiz.question: What does @ServiceConnection provide in Spring Boot 3.1+ Testcontainers tests?
options: It permanently deploys PostgreSQL to production
It disables database migrations
It automatically supplies supported container connection details to Spring Boot
It converts unit tests into E2E tests
quiz.explanation: @ServiceConnection allows Spring Boot to discover connection information from supported Testcontainers services and configure the application accordingly.

quiz.question: Why can relying on @Transactional rollback be insufficient for test isolation?
options: Transactions cannot contain INSERT statements
Rollback only affects work within the relevant transaction boundary
PostgreSQL does not support transactions
JUnit disables transactions automatically
quiz.explanation: Work performed in separate transactions, asynchronous operations, or external systems may not be part of the transaction that the test rolls back.

quiz.question: What does a MockMvc test allow you to check?
options: Only Java syntax
Only PostgreSQL indexes
Only React component state
Spring MVC request handling and responses without requiring a real browser
quiz.explanation: MockMvc can send simulated HTTP requests through Spring MVC and lets you assert status codes, JSON responses, validation behaviour, and other web-layer behaviour.

exercise.title: Build an isolated integration-test harness
exercise.task: Build `withTestApp(testFn)` to simulate the lifecycle of an integration test environment without Docker. The supplied `Db` class represents a tiny in-memory database using Maps, and `createApp(db)` returns an application object with `handle(request)` for `POST /api/tasks` and `GET /api/tasks`. The application validates task creation: a missing or empty `title` must result in HTTP 400. Your `withTestApp(testFn)` must create a brand-new `Db` and app for every call, seed the database with exactly two tasks before running the test, then call `await testFn(app, db)`. It must always clean up by setting `db.closed = true` in a `finally` block, even when `testFn` throws. If `testFn` throws, the error must be rethrown after cleanup. The tests will call `withTestApp` multiple times to verify that writes in one test are not visible in another, that the two seed tasks are available, that cleanup happens after both success and failure, and that test requests actually go through the application's validation rather than bypassing it.
exercise.hint: Create `Db` and `app` inside `withTestApp`, seed the two tasks before the callback runs, then put `await testFn(app, db)` inside `try`. The `finally` block must set `db.closed = true`, and JavaScript will automatically rethrow an error from the `try` block if you do not catch it.

tests.name: It seeds two tasks
tests.code: let observed; await withTestApp(async (app, db) => { observed = await app.handle({ method: "GET", path: "/api/tasks" }); }); return observed.status === 200 && observed.body.length === 2 && observed.body[0].title === "Seed task 1" && observed.body[1].title === "Seed task 2";

tests.name: It isolates writes between calls
tests.code: let firstCount; let secondCount; await withTestApp(async (app) => { await app.handle({ method: "POST", path: "/api/tasks", body: { title: "Only in first test" } }); const response = await app.handle({ method: "GET", path: "/api/tasks" }); firstCount = response.body.length; }); await withTestApp(async (app) => { const response = await app.handle({ method: "GET", path: "/api/tasks" }); secondCount = response.body.length; }); return firstCount === 3 && secondCount === 2;

tests.name: It creates a fresh database each time
tests.code: let firstDb; let secondDb; await withTestApp(async (app, db) => { firstDb = db; }); await withTestApp(async (app, db) => { secondDb = db; }); return firstDb !== secondDb;

tests.name: It cleans up after success
tests.code: let observedDb; await withTestApp(async (app, db) => { observedDb = db; }); return observedDb.closed === true;

tests.name: It cleans up after a failure
tests.code: let observedDb; let rethrown = false; try { await withTestApp(async (app, db) => { observedDb = db; throw new Error("test failure"); }); } catch (error) { rethrown = error instanceof Error && error.message === "test failure"; } return rethrown && observedDb && observedDb.closed === true;

tests.name: It preserves the original test result
tests.code: const result = await withTestApp(async (app) => { return { passed: true, value: 42 }; }); return result.passed === true && result.value === 42;

tests.name: It sends valid requests through the app
tests.code: let response; await withTestApp(async (app) => { response = await app.handle({ method: "POST", path: "/api/tasks", body: { title: "  New task  " } }); }); return response.status === 201 && response.body.title === "New task";

tests.name: It preserves validation errors
tests.code: let response; await withTestApp(async (app) => { response = await app.handle({ method: "POST", path: "/api/tasks", body: { title: "   " } }); }); return response.status === 400 && response.body.error === "Title is required";

tests.name: It does not seed through the request API
tests.code: let response; await withTestApp(async (app) => { response = await app.handle({ method: "GET", path: "/api/tasks" }); }); return response.body.every(task => task.title === "Seed task 1" || task.title === "Seed task 2");
